lessons.title: Investigation & Research Methods
lessons.description: How designers use primary and secondary research to identify user needs and write effective design briefs.
lessons.content_html:
Why Research Matters in Design

Every successful product begins with research. Before a designer picks up a pencil or opens CAD software, they need to understand who they are designing for, what problem they are solving, and what already exists on the market. You need to understand how primary data and secondary data are used to inform the design process.

Key Fact

Primary data is gathered first-hand (surveys, interviews, testing), while secondary data comes from existing sources (books, websites, databases). Designers use both to build a complete picture of user needs.

Primary Research Techniques

Primary research gives designers direct, up-to-date information about their target users.

Market research involves collecting data about consumer preferences, buying habits, and existing products. Designers use questionnaires, online surveys, and face-to-face interviews to gather opinions directly from potential users. Interviews are particularly useful because the designer can ask follow-up questions and observe body language, giving richer data than a written survey alone.

When analysing questionnaire responses, designers create frequency tables to identify patterns. For example, if 80% of respondents say they want a lightweight product, that becomes a key specification point.

Ergonomics is the study of how people interact with products. Designers consider factors like grip size, viewing angles, and reach distances to ensure products are comfortable and safe to use. Anthropometric data provides body measurements from large population samples — heights, hand spans, sitting heights — that help designers size their products appropriately.

Percentiles divide the population into 100 groups by measurement. Most products are designed for the 5th to 95th percentile, meaning they suit 90% of the population. A chair designed only for the 50th percentile (average) would be uncomfortable for both shorter and taller users.

Focus Groups & Product Analysis

Focus groups bring together a small group of target users to discuss a design concept or existing product. The designer facilitates the discussion and records responses. This qualitative data reveals attitudes and feelings that surveys often miss. Product analysis involves systematically evaluating existing products against criteria such as function, aesthetics, cost, materials, and environmental impact.

Key Fact

Product analysis helps designers identify strengths and weaknesses in existing solutions. By comparing products using a comparative chart of performance criteria, designers can spot gaps in the market and opportunities for improvement.

Secondary Research Sources

Secondary research uses information that already exists. This includes published books, academic journals, manufacturer datasheets, government statistics, and online databases. It is quicker and cheaper than primary research but may be out of date or not specific to the designer’s exact needs. The best approach combines both types — secondary research to build background knowledge, then primary research to fill gaps.

Writing a Design Brief & Specification

Once research is complete, the designer writes a design brief — a concise statement of the problem and the proposed solution. This is followed by a detailed design specification listing measurable criteria the product must meet, such as dimensions, materials, weight limits, target cost, and user requirements.

A good specification is specific and measurable. “The product should be lightweight” is vague. “The product should weigh no more than 500 g” is measurable and testable. Designers may also modify their brief as research reveals new information — this is a normal part of the iterative design process.

Key Fact

A design brief outlines the problem in broad terms. A design specification lists precise, measurable requirements. Both may be revised as the project develops.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Section C of the AQA exam, you may be asked to explain why a designer would use a particular research method. Always link your answer to the type of data it produces and how that data improves the final product. For example, “Anthropometric data allows the designer to size the handle for the 5th to 95th percentile, ensuring it is comfortable for 90% of users.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary data (surveys, interviews, ergonomic testing) gives direct, current information; secondary data (books, databases) provides background context quickly and cheaply.
  • Anthropometric data and percentiles help designers create products that fit the widest range of users.
  • A design brief states the problem; a design specification lists measurable success criteria — both may be modified as the project evolves.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'primary data'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that it is data collected first-hand (1). One mark for an example such as surveys, interviews, or testing (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using questionnaires to gather user opinions.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage: can reach a large number of people quickly / produces quantitative data that is easy to analyse (1) with development (1). Disadvantage: responses may be superficial / respondents may not answer honestly / no opportunity for follow-up questions (1) with development (1).

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a new ergonomic computer mouse. Explain how anthropometric data and percentiles would be used in this project.
practice_questions.marks: Anthropometric data provides hand measurements from a large population sample (1). Percentiles divide the population into groups based on size (1). The designer would use the 5th to 95th percentile range to ensure the mouse fits 90% of users (1). This means the grip width, button spacing, and overall size would accommodate both smaller and larger hands (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might modify their design brief during the investigation stage.
practice_questions.marks: Research may reveal new information about user needs that was not anticipated (1), such as a safety requirement identified through product analysis (1). The brief is modified to reflect a more accurate understanding of the problem (1), which leads to a more effective final product (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer would carry out a product analysis of an existing product.
practice_questions.marks: The designer selects an existing product that addresses a similar need (1). They evaluate it against criteria such as function, aesthetics, cost, materials, and environmental impact (1). They record strengths and weaknesses in a comparative chart (1). This information is used to identify opportunities for improvement in their own design (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of using both primary and secondary research when developing a new product. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough discussion comparing both types with clear justification. E.g., Secondary research provides quick background knowledge of materials, trends, and existing solutions, but may not be specific to the target user. Primary research fills this gap with direct user feedback, ergonomic data, and product testing. Using both gives a comprehensive evidence base, reducing the risk of designing a product that fails to meet user needs.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate discussion of both types with some justification.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points about one or both types with limited justification.

lessons.title: Environmental, Social & Economic Challenges
lessons.description: How environmental, social and economic factors create both opportunities and constraints for designers.
lessons.content_html:
Design in Context

Designers do not work in isolation. Every product they create exists within a web of environmental, social, and economic pressures. The specification requires you to understand how these challenges present both opportunities and constraints that shape the design and manufacturing process.

Environmental Challenges

The environmental impact of products — from raw material extraction through manufacture, use, and disposal — is one of the biggest challenges facing modern designers. The specification highlights three key areas.

Key Fact

The spec names three environmental challenges: deforestation, increased carbon dioxide levels leading to potential global warming, and the need for fair trade. Each of these creates constraints on material choice and manufacturing methods.

Deforestation destroys habitats, reduces biodiversity, and releases stored carbon into the atmosphere. For designers working with timber, this means choosing wood from sustainably managed forests certified by organisations like the FSC (Forest Stewardship Council). Alternatively, designers might select manufactured boards such as MDF or plywood, which use smaller offcuts and waste timber more efficiently.

Manufacturing processes burn fossil fuels and release carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming. Designers can reduce a product’s carbon footprint by choosing low-energy manufacturing methods, sourcing local materials to reduce transport emissions, designing for energy efficiency during use, and making products that last longer so they are replaced less often.

Social Challenges

Social factors influence what people want and need from products. Designers must consider cultural values, ethical concerns, user demographics, and changing lifestyles. An aging population, for example, creates demand for products with larger controls, clearer displays, and easier grip — turning a social challenge into a design opportunity.

Inclusive design aims to make products usable by the widest possible range of people, regardless of age, ability, or background. Products designed inclusively — such as lever-style door handles instead of round knobs — often benefit everyone, not just those with specific needs.

Key Fact

Social challenges such as an aging population, changing cultural trends, and ethical consumer demand create design opportunities. Inclusive design responds to these by making products accessible to the widest range of users.

Economic Challenges

Economic factors shape what materials a designer can afford, where manufacturing takes place, and what price consumers will pay. Key economic challenges include:

  • Material costs — fluctuating raw material prices force designers to find cost-effective alternatives or reduce material usage.
  • Labour costs — manufacturing in countries with lower wages reduces costs but raises ethical concerns about working conditions.
  • Market competition — designers must balance quality and features against a price point that competes with existing products.

The Need for Fair Trade

Fair trade ensures that producers in developing countries receive fair payment and work in safe conditions. Designers selecting materials — such as cotton for textiles or cocoa butter for cosmetic packaging — should consider whether supply chains meet fair trade standards. While fair trade materials may cost more, they appeal to ethically conscious consumers and reduce exploitation.

The 6 Rs of Sustainability

Designers use the 6 Rs framework to minimise environmental impact: Reduce material and energy use, Reuse components or products, Recycle materials at end of life, Refuse harmful or unnecessary materials, Rethink whether the product is needed or could work differently, and Repair rather than replace. Applying these principles from the earliest design stages leads to more sustainable products.

Key Fact

The 6 Rs — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair — guide sustainable design. Applying them from the start of the design process helps minimise environmental impact throughout a product’s life cycle.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about environmental, social, or economic challenges, always link the challenge to a specific design decision. Don’t just say “deforestation is bad” — explain how it constrains material choice (e.g., “the designer would select FSC-certified timber to avoid contributing to deforestation”). The best answers connect the challenge to the opportunity it creates.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Environmental challenges (deforestation, CO2 emissions, fair trade) constrain material and manufacturing choices but also drive innovation in sustainable design.
  • Social challenges such as aging populations and changing lifestyles create opportunities for inclusive and accessible design.
  • The 6 Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair) provide a framework for sustainable design decisions.

practice_questions.text: Give two environmental challenges that influence design decisions.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: deforestation (1), increased carbon dioxide levels / global warming (1), the need for fair trade (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how deforestation creates a constraint for a designer using timber-based materials.
practice_questions.marks: Deforestation reduces availability of hardwoods (1) and damages ecosystems / biodiversity (1). This constrains the designer to use sustainably sourced timber, such as FSC-certified wood (1), or to choose manufactured boards like MDF or plywood which use waste timber more efficiently (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how an aging population creates a design opportunity for a kitchen product manufacturer.
practice_questions.marks: Older users may have reduced grip strength or impaired vision (1). This creates an opportunity to design products with larger handles, non-slip grips, and high-contrast labels (1). Inclusive design features like these also benefit other users (1), potentially expanding the product's market appeal (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer could use the 6 Rs to reduce the environmental impact of a product.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each R correctly applied to a product example, up to 4 marks. E.g., Reduce the amount of packaging material (1), design components to be Reused in future products (1), select materials that can be Recycled at end of life (1), Refuse to use non-recyclable plastics (1), Rethink whether disposable elements are necessary (1), design for Repair so parts can be replaced (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain what fair trade means and why a designer might choose fair trade materials.
practice_questions.marks: Fair trade ensures producers in developing countries receive fair payment and safe working conditions (1). A designer might choose fair trade materials to ensure ethical sourcing (1). This may increase material costs (1) but appeals to ethically conscious consumers and supports responsible supply chains (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss how economic challenges can influence a designer's choice of materials and manufacturing methods. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough discussion linking economic factors to specific design decisions. E.g., Fluctuating material costs may lead a designer to substitute expensive hardwood with manufactured board, reducing cost while maintaining structural performance. Manufacturing in lower-wage countries reduces unit cost but raises ethical concerns. The designer must balance quality, ethics, and price to create a competitive product.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate discussion with some justified examples.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of economic factors with limited justification.

lessons.title: The Work of Others
lessons.description: Investigating the work of influential designers and companies from the AQA specification list.
lessons.content_html:
Learning from Design History

The specification requires you to investigate, analyse, and evaluate the work of past and present designers and companies. Understanding how others have solved design problems helps you develop your own design thinking. You must study at least two designers and two companies from the specification list.

Influential Designers

William Morris was a leading figure in the Arts and Crafts movement. He believed that mass production led to poor quality and that beauty should be part of everyday objects. His textile and wallpaper designs featured intricate, nature-inspired patterns — flowers, birds, and trailing vines — created using traditional hand-printing techniques. Morris’s philosophy that “nothing should be in your houses that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful” still influences design today.

Morris founded Morris & Co. to produce handcrafted furnishings, stained glass, and textiles. His work demonstrates how a designer’s values — in this case, a rejection of industrial mass production — shape both the aesthetic and the manufacturing process of their products.

Philippe Starck is one of the most prolific designers of the modern era. His approach is almost the opposite of Morris’s — he embraces mass production and believes good design should be affordable and accessible to everyone. His Juicy Salif citrus squeezer for Alessi (1990) is a famous example: a sculptural, aluminium spider-like form that functions as a lemon press but is equally seen as an art object.

Starck works across furniture, interiors, consumer electronics, and even architecture. His Louis Ghost Chair (2002), made from transparent polycarbonate, reinterprets a classic 18th-century silhouette using modern materials and manufacturing. Starck demonstrates how designers use new materials and technologies to reimagine traditional forms.

Key Fact

William Morris rejected mass production and valued handcraftsmanship. Philippe Starck embraces it, believing good design should be affordable and accessible. Both have shaped how we think about the relationship between design, manufacturing, and the consumer.

Zaha Hadid was an Iraqi-British architect known for her dramatic, flowing, curvilinear structures that challenged conventional building design. She was the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize (2004). Her buildings — such as the London Aquatics Centre and the Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku — use reinforced concrete and parametric design software to create forms that seem to defy gravity.

Hadid also designed products including furniture, jewellery, and shoes, always characterised by the same fluid, dynamic lines. Her work shows how parametric design and advanced manufacturing (such as CNC milling and 3D printing) allow designers to realise forms that were previously impossible.

Sir Alec Issigonis was a British-Greek automotive engineer best known for designing the original Mini (1959). The Mini was a response to the Suez fuel crisis — a social and economic challenge that demanded a small, fuel-efficient, affordable car. Issigonis placed the engine sideways (transverse) and used front-wheel drive to maximise interior space in a tiny body. His innovative use of space shows how constraints can drive creative engineering solutions.

Influential Companies

Dyson is a British technology company that built its reputation on the bagless cyclone vacuum cleaner. Founder James Dyson famously created 5,127 prototypes before perfecting the design. This exemplifies iterative design — a cycle of testing, evaluating, and improving. Dyson products are characterised by engineering innovation, distinctive aesthetics, and premium pricing. The company invests heavily in research and development, holding thousands of patents.

Apple is famous for its design-led approach, where the user experience drives every decision. Under the influence of former Chief Design Officer Jony Ive, Apple products became known for minimalist aesthetics, precision-machined aluminium bodies, and intuitive interfaces. The company demonstrates how material choice, manufacturing precision, and consistent branding create a premium product identity.

Apple’s approach to user-centred design means products are tested extensively with real users. Features are removed rather than added — simplicity is a core principle. This contrasts with companies that compete on features, showing there are multiple valid approaches to product design.

Key Fact

Dyson demonstrates iterative design through extensive prototyping and engineering innovation. Apple demonstrates user-centred design through minimalist aesthetics and intuitive interfaces. Both invest heavily in R&D to maintain their market position.

Material Categories in Design

the specification lists six material categories that designers work with. Each designer and company above uses different materials depending on the product type:

  • Papers and boards — used in packaging design, prototyping, and graphic products.
  • Timber-based materials — hardwoods, softwoods, and manufactured boards used in furniture and construction (Morris).
  • Metal-based materials — ferrous and non-ferrous metals used in engineering and product design (Starck’s Juicy Salif uses cast aluminium).
  • Polymers — thermoplastics and thermosets used in consumer products (Starck’s Ghost Chair uses polycarbonate; Dyson uses ABS and polypropylene).
  • Textile-based materials — natural and synthetic fabrics used in fashion, interiors, and technical products (Morris’s printed fabrics).
  • Electronic and mechanical systems — circuits, motors, sensors, and mechanisms used in smart products (Dyson’s digital motors; Apple’s integrated electronics).
Key Fact

The six AQA material categories are: papers and boards, timber-based materials, metal-based materials, polymers, textile-based materials, and electronic and mechanical systems. You must study at least one category in depth for your NEA.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about designers and companies often ask you to “analyse” or “evaluate” their work. This means going beyond description — explain why their design choices were effective and how their work could inform your own designing. For example, don’t just say Starck used polycarbonate — explain that it allowed mass production of a complex form at lower cost than traditional materials.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • William Morris championed handcraftsmanship and natural forms; Philippe Starck embraces mass production to make design accessible; Zaha Hadid used parametric design to create fluid architectural forms; Issigonis showed how constraints drive innovation.
  • Dyson exemplifies iterative design through engineering and prototyping; Apple demonstrates user-centred design through simplicity and material quality.
  • The six material categories (papers/boards, timber, metals, polymers, textiles, electronic/mechanical systems) span the full range of design and technology.

practice_questions.text: Name two designers from the AQA specification list and state one material category each is associated with.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per correct designer-material pairing. E.g., William Morris — textile-based materials (1), Philippe Starck — polymers / metal-based materials (1). Accept any valid pairing from the specification list.

practice_questions.text: Explain how William Morris's design philosophy influenced his choice of materials and manufacturing methods.
practice_questions.marks: Morris valued handcraftsmanship over mass production (1). He used natural materials such as hand-printed fabrics and hand-carved wood (1). He rejected industrial manufacturing in favour of traditional techniques (1). This was driven by his belief that mass production reduced quality and separated the maker from the product (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Philippe Starck's Juicy Salif demonstrates the relationship between form, function, and manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks: The Juicy Salif has a sculptural, spider-like form that is visually striking (1). It functions as a citrus squeezer but is also considered an art object (1). It is made from cast aluminium, allowing complex shapes through mass production (1). This demonstrates Starck's belief that functional products can also be aesthetically ambitious and affordable (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how Dyson's approach to product development demonstrates iterative design.
practice_questions.marks: Iterative design involves repeated cycles of testing, evaluation, and improvement (1). James Dyson created 5,127 prototypes of his cyclone vacuum (1). Each prototype was tested, and problems were identified and fixed in the next version (1). This resulted in a highly refined product that outperformed competitors (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the design approaches of Dyson and Apple. Explain one similarity and one difference.
practice_questions.marks: Similarity: Both invest heavily in R&D / both focus on premium products / both prioritise quality (1) with development (1). Difference: Dyson focuses on engineering innovation and visible technology, while Apple prioritises minimalist aesthetics and hides complexity from the user (1) with development (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how studying the work of past and present designers helps students develop their own design ideas. Justify your answer with examples.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough evaluation with justified examples. E.g., Studying Morris shows how personal values shape material choices; studying Starck shows how new materials enable new forms; studying Dyson shows the value of persistent prototyping. These examples provide strategies students can apply to their own NEA work, such as iterative testing or using material properties creatively.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate evaluation with some examples.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statement about learning from others with limited examples.

lessons.title: Design Strategies & Communication
lessons.description: Applying design strategies like iteration and collaboration, and communicating ideas through drawings and models.
lessons.content_html:
Design Strategies

The specification requires you to understand how different strategies help designers generate creative ideas and develop them into successful products. A strategy is a planned approach to solving a design problem — choosing the right one depends on the nature of the brief, the client, and the context.

Collaboration involves working with others — other designers, engineers, clients, or end users — to develop ideas. It brings together different skills and viewpoints, often producing solutions that no individual would have reached alone. In industry, product design teams typically include specialists in materials, electronics, marketing, and manufacturing.

User-centred design places the end user at the heart of every decision. The designer gathers data through interviews, observation, and usability testing, then designs specifically around those findings. This reduces the risk of creating something that looks good but fails in practice. Apple’s product design is a well-known example of this approach.

A systems approach breaks a complex product down into manageable sub-systems — typically input, process, and output. Each sub-system is designed and tested separately, then integrated. This is common in electronic and mechanical products. For example, an automatic hand dryer has an input (motion sensor), a process (control circuit), and outputs (heater element and fan motor).

Key Fact

The five design strategies named in the specification are: collaboration, user-centred design, a systems approach, iterative design, and avoiding design fixation.

Iterative Design & Avoiding Design Fixation

Iterative design involves repeated cycles of designing, making, testing, and evaluating. Rather than trying to produce a perfect solution first time, the designer creates quick prototypes, tests them, learns from the results, and refines the design. Each cycle gets closer to the final solution.

Design fixation occurs when a designer becomes too attached to an early idea and stops exploring alternatives. To avoid it, designers use techniques such as brainstorming, mind mapping, SCAMPER (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse), and looking at the problem from different perspectives.

Communicating Design Ideas

AQA requires you to develop, communicate, record, and justify your design ideas using a range of techniques. The method you choose depends on the audience and purpose.

Freehand sketching is used in the early stages to quickly explore ideas. Sketches are fast, informal, and often annotated with notes explaining materials, dimensions, or functions.

Isometric drawing shows a 3D view of an object with all three axes visible. Measurements are to scale, making it useful for communicating shape and proportion. Perspective drawing creates a more realistic view by using vanishing points, making objects appear to recede into the distance.

Third-angle orthographic projection is a formal engineering drawing showing front, side, and plan views. It uses conventions such as dimension lines, centre lines, and hidden detail (dashed lines), all drawn to scale. This is the standard format for working drawings that go to a manufacturer.

Exploded diagrams show how parts fit together by separating them along an axis, revealing assembly order and constructional detail. System and schematic diagrams show the logical relationships between components — circuit diagrams are a common example.

Computer-based tools include CAD (Computer Aided Design) software such as SolidWorks, Fusion 360, or 2D Design. These allow precise modelling, rendering, and even simulation of how a product will behave. Mathematical modelling uses calculations or simulations to test performance before building a physical prototype.

Physical modelling involves making 3D models from card, foam, fabric (toile), or breadboard circuits. Models help test form, proportion, and ergonomics in ways that drawings cannot.

Key Fact

Communication methods range from quick freehand sketches (idea generation) to formal third-angle orthographic projections (manufacture). The choice depends on the stage of the design process and the audience.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked about design strategies, don’t just define them — explain when and why each one would be used. For communication questions, identify the purpose (exploring ideas vs. giving to a manufacturer) and match it to the appropriate technique (freehand sketch vs. orthographic projection).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five AQA design strategies are collaboration, user-centred design, systems approach, iterative design, and avoiding design fixation.
  • Iterative design uses repeated cycles of designing, making, testing, and evaluating to refine a product.
  • Communication methods range from freehand sketches and isometric drawings (early stages) to third-angle orthographic projection and CAD models (manufacture-ready).

lessons.title: Prototype Development & Evaluation
lessons.description: How designers develop, test, and evaluate prototypes to meet client needs and demonstrate innovation.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Prototype?

A prototype is a working model or test version of a product. In AQA Design & Technology, the term can describe either a physical product or a system (such as an electronic circuit). Prototypes allow designers to test ideas in the real world, identify problems, and refine their designs before committing to full-scale manufacture.

Developing Prototypes

The specification states that prototypes must be developed in response to client wants and needs. A successful prototype should satisfy the requirements of the design brief, respond to what the client has asked for, demonstrate innovation, be functional, consider aesthetics, and be potentially marketable.

Key Fact

A well-developed prototype must: (1) satisfy the requirements of the brief, (2) respond to client wants and needs, (3) demonstrate innovation, (4) be functional, (5) consider aesthetics, and (6) be potentially marketable.

Designers use different types of prototype depending on what they need to test:

  • Appearance models — show the form, colour, and surface finish of a product but may not be functional. Often made from foam, card, or 3D-printed materials.
  • Functional prototypes — work as intended, allowing the designer to test mechanisms, circuits, or moving parts. They may not look like the final product.
  • Production prototypes — closely resemble the final product in both appearance and function. Used for final testing and client approval before manufacturing begins.

Rapid prototyping uses technologies like 3D printing (additive manufacturing), laser cutting, and CNC machining to produce physical models quickly and cheaply. A designer can go from a CAD model to a physical prototype in hours, test it, modify the digital file, and print an improved version the same day. This dramatically speeds up the iterative design process.

CAM (Computer Aided Manufacture) uses CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machines that read digital design files and cut, shape, or build components with high precision and repeatability. In combination with CAD, this enables a seamless digital workflow from design to manufacture.

Evaluating Prototypes

Evaluation is a continuous process, not just a final step. The specification requires students to evaluate prototypes by reflecting critically on their work, responding to feedback, suggesting modifications, and assessing fitness for purpose.

Key Fact

AQA expects you to: (1) reflect critically on your prototype, responding to feedback; (2) suggest modifications to improve it through inception and manufacture; and (3) assess whether the prototype is fit for purpose.

Testing Against the Specification

The design specification written during the investigation stage becomes the evaluation checklist. Each criterion — dimensions, weight, materials, function, aesthetics — is tested against the prototype. Where the prototype falls short, the designer identifies what went wrong and proposes specific improvements. This testing-and-improvement cycle continues until the product meets all specification requirements or the best possible compromise is reached.

Client & User Feedback

Effective evaluation includes feedback from the client and target users, not just the designer’s own assessment. This might involve user testing sessions, questionnaires, or interviews. Third-party feedback often reveals issues the designer has overlooked — for example, a handle that feels comfortable to the designer might be too small for users with larger hands.

Key Fact

Testing with real users reveals problems the designer may not notice. Third-party feedback is essential because the designer is too close to the project to be fully objective.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In evaluation questions, always structure your answer around the specification criteria. State the criterion, explain how you tested it, give the result, and suggest a modification if the prototype fell short. This shows the examiner you can evaluate systematically, not just offer vague opinions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prototypes must satisfy the brief, respond to client needs, demonstrate innovation, be functional, consider aesthetics, and be potentially marketable.
  • Rapid prototyping (3D printing, laser cutting, CNC) accelerates the iterative design cycle by allowing quick physical testing.
  • Evaluation involves testing against the specification, reflecting critically on feedback, suggesting modifications, and assessing fitness for purpose.

lessons.title: Tolerances & Material Management
lessons.description: Working accurately with tolerances, selecting materials, and minimising waste through efficient cutting and marking out.
lessons.content_html:
Selecting Materials & Components

Choosing the right material for a prototype is one of the most important decisions a designer makes. The specification requires you to consider three key factors when selecting materials and components: functional need, cost, and availability.

Functional need comes first — the material must be suitable for the job. A structural component needs strength and rigidity, while a handle needs good grip and comfort. Cost matters because designers work within budgets, and availability determines whether the material can be sourced in the right stock forms and quantities.

Key Fact

Material selection is based on three factors: functional need (does the material perform the required task?), cost (is it within budget?), and availability (can it be sourced in appropriate stock forms?).

Understanding Tolerances

A tolerance is the acceptable range of variation in a measurement. No manufacturing process is perfectly precise, so tolerances define how much a dimension can vary and still produce a functional product. the specification uses the example of ±2 mm for general workshop tolerances.

Different materials and processes require different tolerances:

  • Timber — general tolerance of ±2 mm for hand-cut joints. CNC-cut timber can achieve much tighter tolerances.
  • Metals — precision engineering may require tolerances of ±0.1 mm or tighter, especially for components that must fit together exactly.
  • Textiles — seam allowances (typically 10–15 mm) act as a form of tolerance, ensuring there is enough material for stitching without the garment being too tight or too loose.
  • Electronics — resistor tolerances are given as a percentage (e.g., ±5% for a standard carbon film resistor), indicated by a coloured band on the component.
Key Fact

A tolerance of ±2 mm means a component can be up to 2 mm larger or smaller than the specified dimension and still be acceptable. Tolerances ensure parts fit together correctly and the product functions as intended.

Material Management — Minimising Waste

The specification emphasises the importance of planning the cutting and shaping of materials to minimise waste. This is both an economic consideration (wasted material is wasted money) and an environmental one (less waste means a smaller environmental footprint).

Nesting is the practice of arranging shapes as closely together as possible on a sheet of material before cutting. CNC machines and laser cutters can use software to optimise nesting automatically. Designers must also account for material removed by the cutting method — a saw blade removes a kerf width of material, and this must be factored into measurements.

For textiles, pattern pieces are laid out on fabric to minimise offcuts. The grain direction of the fabric must also be considered, as cutting across the grain can affect the way the garment hangs and stretches.

Marking Out Methods

Accurate marking out is essential for working within tolerances. The specification requires understanding of reference datum points, coordinates, templates, jigs, and patterns.

A datum point is a fixed reference from which all other measurements are taken. Using a single datum reduces cumulative errors. Jigs hold workpieces in position and guide cutting tools, ensuring repeatability when making multiple identical parts. Templates and patterns are particularly important in textile work, where paper patterns are pinned to fabric before cutting.

Designers calculate material requirements using surface area and volume. For flat materials (sheet metal, plywood, fabric), the total area of all parts plus waste allowance determines how much material to order. For 3D products, volume calculations help estimate material mass and cost. All calculations should use SI units (millimetres for dimensions, grams or kilograms for mass).

Key Fact

Nesting arranges parts as closely together as possible on a material sheet to minimise waste. Combined with accurate marking out from a datum point, it ensures efficient use of materials and reduces both cost and environmental impact.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Tolerance questions often ask you to explain why tolerances are applied rather than just what they are. Always link your answer to the function of the product: “If the tolerance is exceeded, the two components will not fit together, and the mechanism will jam.” Showing the consequence of exceeding a tolerance demonstrates deeper understanding.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Material selection considers functional need, cost, and availability; components must be sourced in appropriate commercial stock forms.
  • Tolerances define the acceptable range of variation in dimensions (e.g., ±2 mm) and differ across material categories.
  • Material management includes nesting, kerf allowance, datum-based marking out, and calculating material requirements in SI units to minimise waste.

lessons.title: Specialist Tools, Equipment & Processes
lessons.description: Selecting and using specialist tools, techniques, and surface finishes safely to create quality prototypes.
lessons.content_html:
Specialist Tools & Equipment

The specification requires you to understand how to select and use specialist tools and equipment — including hand tools, machinery, and digital manufacturing — appropriate to the material and task. Crucially, you must also demonstrate that you can use them safely to protect yourself and others.

Hand tools are powered by the user rather than electricity. They give precise control and are essential for detailed work. Key examples include:

  • Marking and measuring — steel rule, try square, marking gauge, scriber, engineer’s square. Accurate marking out is the foundation of quality work.
  • Cutting — tenon saw, coping saw, hacksaw, craft knife, scissors. The choice depends on the material: a tenon saw for timber, a hacksaw for metal, scissors for textiles.
  • Shaping — chisels, planes, files, rasps. Files come in different profiles (flat, half-round, round, triangular) for different shapes.
  • Joining — screwdrivers, hammers, clamps, soldering iron. Clamps hold work securely while adhesive dries or while drilling.

Power tools and workshop machinery increase speed, accuracy, and capability beyond what hand tools can achieve:

  • Pillar drill — drills precise, vertical holes. Always secured with a machine vice or clamp; never hold work by hand.
  • Band saw — cuts curves in timber and some plastics. Blade guard adjusted to just above the workpiece.
  • Wood lathe — turns cylindrical shapes from timber. Requires a face shield, no loose clothing, and hair tied back.
  • Sewing machine — joins fabric quickly and consistently using a lockstitch mechanism.
Key Fact

Workshop safety essentials: always wear appropriate PPE (safety glasses, apron, hearing protection), secure workpieces with clamps or vices, never leave machines running unattended, keep guards in place, and ensure no loose clothing, jewellery, or untied hair near rotating machinery.

Digital Design & Manufacture

CAD (Computer Aided Design) allows designers to create, modify, and test designs digitally before any material is cut. CAM (Computer Aided Manufacture) converts those digital files into physical products using CNC machines, laser cutters, and 3D printers.

CNC routing/milling uses a computer-controlled cutting tool to carve shapes from solid material. It is a wastage process — material is removed to create the shape.

Laser cutting uses a focused laser beam to cut or engrave sheet materials (acrylic, MDF, plywood, card) with extremely high precision. It produces clean edges with minimal kerf.

3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds objects layer by layer. Common types include FDM (Fused Deposition Modelling) using thermoplastic filament and SLA (Stereolithography) using UV-cured resin. 3D printing is ideal for complex shapes that would be difficult to create by traditional methods.

Specialist Techniques & Processes

Manufacturing processes are grouped into four categories based on how they shape material:

  • Wastage — material is removed (cutting, drilling, milling, turning, filing).
  • Addition — material is joined together (welding, soldering, brazing, adhesives, sewing, laminating).
  • Deforming — material is permanently reshaped without adding or removing (bending, press forming, vacuum forming, forging).
  • Reforming — material is melted or dissolved and reformed into a new shape (casting, injection moulding, blow moulding, extrusion).
Key Fact

The four manufacturing process categories are wastage (material removed), addition (material joined), deforming (material reshaped), and reforming (material melted and reshaped). The correct process depends on the material, the shape required, and the production scale.

Surface Treatments & Finishes

Surface treatments and finishes are applied for both functional and aesthetic reasons. Functional finishes protect against corrosion, moisture, UV damage, or wear. Aesthetic finishes improve the look and feel of the product.

Examples include: paint and lacquer (wood, metal), varnish and oil (wood), powder coating (metal), anodising (aluminium), electroplating (metal), and dyeing (textiles). The choice depends on the material, the intended use, and the level of protection required.

Key Fact

Surface finishes serve functional purposes (protection from corrosion, moisture, or wear), aesthetic purposes (colour, texture, sheen), or both. Selecting the right finish is part of designing a quality product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about tools and processes often give you a scenario and ask you to justify your choice. Always name the specific tool or process, explain why it is suitable for the material and task, and mention a safety precaution you would take. This three-part structure — name, justify, safety — covers all the marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Specialist tools include hand tools, power tools, and digital manufacturing equipment (CNC, laser cutters, 3D printers) — each chosen to match the material and task.
  • Manufacturing processes are categorised as wastage, addition, deforming, or reforming, depending on how material is shaped.
  • Surface treatments and finishes protect products and improve their appearance; the choice depends on material, function, and aesthetics.

practice_questions.text: Name one hand tool and one machine tool suitable for cutting timber, and state one safety precaution for each.
practice_questions.marks: Hand tool: e.g., tenon saw (1). Safety: secure workpiece in a vice, cut on the waste side of the line (1). Machine tool: e.g., band saw (1). Safety: adjust blade guard to just above the workpiece, keep fingers clear of the blade (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between CAD and CAM.
practice_questions.marks: CAD (Computer Aided Design) uses software to create digital 2D or 3D models of a product (1). The designer can modify, test, and render designs on screen (1). CAM (Computer Aided Manufacture) uses computer-controlled machines to produce physical products from digital files (1). Examples include CNC routing, laser cutting, and 3D printing (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using 3D printing to make a prototype.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage: Can produce complex shapes that would be difficult with traditional methods (1), and allows quick iteration from a CAD file (1). Disadvantage: Limited material options compared to traditional manufacturing — usually only thermoplastics or resins (1), and surface finish may require post-processing such as sanding (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the four categories of manufacturing process, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Wastage — material is removed, e.g., drilling (1). Addition — material is joined, e.g., soldering (1). Deforming — material is permanently reshaped, e.g., vacuum forming (1). Reforming — material is melted and reshaped, e.g., injection moulding (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose to anodise an aluminium product rather than paint it.
practice_questions.marks: Anodising creates a hard, durable oxide layer on the aluminium surface (1). This provides better corrosion and wear resistance than paint (1). The anodised layer can be dyed in various colours for aesthetic appeal (1). Unlike paint, anodising does not chip or peel because it becomes part of the metal surface (1).

practice_questions.text: A designer needs to produce 500 identical plastic casings for an electronic product. Discuss whether 3D printing or injection moulding would be more suitable. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough discussion. E.g., 3D printing does not require a mould, so setup costs are low, but each unit takes time to print and finish — suitable for small batches only. Injection moulding requires an expensive steel mould (high setup cost) but produces each unit in seconds with excellent consistency and surface finish. For 500 units, injection moulding is more cost-effective overall because the per-unit cost drops sharply once the mould is made. 3D printing would only be preferable for very small quantities or complex geometries that cannot be moulded.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate discussion with some comparison.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of one method with limited justification.

glossary_terms.definition: Computer Aided Design — the use of software to create precise 2D or 3D digital models of a product.
Computer Aided Manufacture — manufacturing controlled by computer software using CNC machines, laser cutters, and 3D printers.
Computer Numerical Control — a subtractive process where a computer-controlled tool cuts material from a solid block.
An additive manufacturing process that builds objects layer by layer from a digital file.
A manufacturing technique that removes material to create the desired shape, such as cutting or drilling.
A manufacturing technique that joins materials together, such as welding, soldering, or adhesives.
A manufacturing technique that permanently reshapes material without adding or removing it, such as bending or vacuum forming.
A manufacturing technique that melts or dissolves material and reshapes it, such as casting or injection moulding.
A coating or treatment applied for protection or to improve appearance, such as paint, varnish, or anodising.
